exampleAnswers.title: Calculating Inverse Trigonometric Function Integrals Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows: \begin{align} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7 - (2x + 4)^2}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7(1 - (2x + 4)^2/7)}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7} \cdot \sqrt{1 - (2x + 4)^2/7}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (2x + 4)^2/7}} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - ( (2x+4)/\sqrt{7} )^2}} \, \textrm{d}x \end{align}

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine: \[ \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u + C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{2x+4}{\sqrt{7}}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u=\dfrac{2x+4}{\sqrt{7}}. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{7}} \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7 - (2x + 4)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - ( (2x+4)/\sqrt{7} )^2}} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{7}} \int \dfrac {1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{7}}{2} \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2} \arcsin{u} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{2}\arcsin\left(\dfrac{2x+4}{\sqrt{7}} \right) + C \end{align}

example.title: Calculating Inverse Trigonometric Function Integrals Using Substitution

question.explanation:
Let's rewrite our integral as follows: \begin{align} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9 - (6x - 2)^2}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9(1 - (6x -2)^2/9)}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9} \cdot \sqrt{1 - (6x-2)^2/9}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{1 - (6x-2)^2/9}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (6x-2)^2/9}} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{3} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - ( (6x-2)/3 )^2}} \, \textrm{d}x \end{align}

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine: \[ \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u + C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{6x-2}{3}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u=\dfrac{6x-2}{3}. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x} = 2 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \textrm{d}x = \dfrac{1}{2}\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: \begin{align} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{9 - (6x-2)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{3} \int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - ( (6x-2)/3 )^2}} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{3} \int \dfrac {1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{6} \arcsin{u} + C\\[5pt] & = \dfrac{1}{6}\arcsin\left(\dfrac{6x-2}{3} \right) + C \end{align}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing an Arctangent Integral by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square in the denominator: \[ \eqalign{ x^2+4x+13 & = x^2 + 2 \cdot 2x+ (2^2 - 2^2) + 13 \\[3pt] & = (x^2+ 2 \cdot 2x+ 2^2) - 4 + 13 \\[3pt] & = (x+2)^2+9 } \]

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get \begin{align*} \int \dfrac{1}{x^2+4x+13} \, \textrm{d}x &=\int \dfrac{1}{(x+2)^2+9} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{9} \int \dfrac{1}{ 1 + ((x+2)/3)^2 } \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent: \[ \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan u + C. \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x+2}{3}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution

\[ u=\dfrac{x+2}{3}. \] Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{3} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x =3\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ \int \dfrac{1}{x^2 + 4x + 13} \, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{1}{9} \int \dfrac{1}{ 1+( (x+2)/3 )^2 } \, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1}{9} \int \dfrac{1 }{1+u^2} \cdot 3 \, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {1}{3}\int \dfrac{1 }{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] & =\dfrac {1}{3} \arctan u + C \\[5pt] & =\dfrac {1}{3} \arctan\left(\dfrac {x+2} {3} \right) + C } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Computing an Arctangent Integral by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square in the denominator: \[ \eqalign{ x^2-4x+5 &= x^2-2 \cdot 2x+(2^2-2^2)+5 \\[5pt] &= (x^2-2 \cdot 2x+2^2)-4+5 \\[5pt] & =(x-2)^2+1 } \]

Substituting the above into the denominator, we get \begin{align*} \int \dfrac{3}{x^2-4x+5} \, \textrm{d}x &=\int \dfrac{3}{(x-2)^2+1} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3 \int \dfrac{1}{ 1 + (x-2)^2 } \, \textrm{d}x \end{align*}

This resembles the basic integral for inverse tangent: \[ \int \dfrac{1}{1+u^2} \, \textrm{d}u = \arctan u + C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $(x-2).$

So, let's perform the substitution

\[ u=x-2. \] Differentiating, we get

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u. \]

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $2$ $3$
$u$ $0$ $1$

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate:

\[ \eqalign{ \int_{2}^{3} \dfrac{3}{x^2-4x+5}\, \textrm{d}x &= 3\int_{2}^{3} \dfrac{1}{1+(x-2)^2}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3\int_{0}^{1} \dfrac{1}{1+u^2}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=3\arctan u\,\Bigg|_{0}^{1}\\[5pt] &=3(\arctan{1} -\arctan{0}) \\[5pt] &=3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}-0\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}. } \]

exampleAnswers.title: Computing an Arcsine Integral by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: \begin{align*} -x^2 + 2x + 3 & = -(x^2 - 2x) + 3 \\[5pt] & = -( (x^2 - 2x + 1) - 1) + 3\\[5pt] & = -( (x-1)^2 - 1) + 3\\[5pt] & = -(x-1)^2 + 1 + 3\\[5pt] & = 4 - (x-1)^2 \end{align*}

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get \begin{align*} \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{-x^2 + 2x + 3}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{4 - (x-1)^2} } \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt {4(1 - (x-1)^2/4)} }\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & = \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{4} \cdot \sqrt {1 - (x-1)^2/2^2} }\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] %& = \int \dfrac{3}{2\cdot\sqrt {1 - (x-1)^2/2^2} }\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] & =\dfrac{3}{2} \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{ 1 - ( (x-1)/2)^2 }}\, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine: \[ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u +C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac {x-1}{2}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u = \dfrac {x-1}{2}. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac12 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = 2\textrm{d}u. \]

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $1-\sqrt{3}$ $1+\sqrt{3}$
$u$ $-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ $\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Therefore, \begin{align*} \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{3}{\sqrt{-x^2 + 2x + 3} } \, \textrm{d}x & = \dfrac{3}{2} \int_{1-\sqrt{3}}^{1+\sqrt{3}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{ 1 - ( (x-1)/2)^2 }}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{2}\int_{-\sqrt{3}/2}^{\sqrt{3}/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \cdot 2\textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &=3\int_{-\sqrt3/2}^{\sqrt3/2} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= 3 \arcsin u \, \bigg|_{-\sqrt3/2}^{\sqrt3/2}\\[5pt] &=3\left(\arcsin{\left(\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)}-\arcsin{\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt3}2\right)}\right) \\[5pt] &= 3\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} - \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\right)\\[5pt] &= 2\pi. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: \begin{align*} -2x^2-12x+8&= -2\left(x^2 +6x -4 \right) \\[5pt] &= -2\left(x^2 +2 \cdot 3x + \left[3^2 - 3^2\right]-4 \right) \\[5pt] %&= -2\left[(x^2 +6x + 9) -9-4 \right] \\[5pt] & = -2\left(\left(x+3 \right) ^2 -13 \right)\\[5pt] & = 2\left(13-\left(x+3 \right) ^2 \right) \end{align*}

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get \begin{align*} \int \dfrac{22}{\sqrt{-2x^2-12x+18}}\, \textrm{d}x & =\int \dfrac{22}{\sqrt{2(13-(x+3) ^2)}}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & =\int \dfrac{22}{\sqrt{26(1-(x+3) ^2/13)}}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & =\int \dfrac{22}{\sqrt{26} \cdot \sqrt{1-(x+3) ^2/13)}}\, \textrm{d}x\\[5pt] & = \dfrac {22}{\sqrt{26}}\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+3)/ \sqrt{13})^2}}\, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

This resembles the basic integral for inverse sine: \[ \int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\,\textrm{d}u = \arcsin u+C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $\left(\dfrac{x+3}{\sqrt{ 13}}\right).$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u =\dfrac{x+3}{\sqrt{ 13}}. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac1{\sqrt{ 13}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \sqrt{13}\,\textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: \[\eqalign{ \int \dfrac{22}{\sqrt{-2x^2-12x+18}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \dfrac {22}{\sqrt{26}}\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-(x+3)/ \sqrt{13})^2}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {22}{\sqrt{26}}\int \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1-u^2}}\cdot \sqrt{13}\,\textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {22}{\sqrt {2} } \int \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\sqrt{1-u^2}} \\[5pt] &= 11\sqrt 2 \arcsin{ u} + C\\[5pt] &= 11\sqrt 2 \arcsin\left( \dfrac {x+3}{\sqrt {13} } \right) + C. }\]

exampleAnswers.title: Computing an Arcsecant Integral by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root: \begin{align*} x^2-12x+35&= x^2 -2 \cdot 6x +(6^2-6^2)+35\\[5pt] &= (x^2 -12x +36)-36+35\\[5pt] &= (x-6)^2-1 \\ \end{align*}

Substituting the above in the given integral, we get \[ \int \dfrac{10}{|x-6|\sqrt{x^2-12x+35}}\, \textrm{d}x = 10 \int \dfrac{1}{|x-6|\sqrt{(x-6)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x . \]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant:

\[ \int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec} \, u +C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x-6.$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u=x-6. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u. \]

Finally, we write the integral in terms of $u,$ and evaluate: \begin{align*} \int \dfrac{10}{|x-6|\sqrt{x^2-12x+35}}\, \textrm{d}x &= 10 \int \dfrac{1}{|x-6|\sqrt{(x-6)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 10 \int \dfrac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= 10\, \textrm{arcsec }{ u} + C \\[5pt] &=10\, \textrm{arcsec}{ (x-6)} + C. \end{align*}

example.title: Computing an Arcsecant Integral by Completing the Square

question.explanation:
First, we complete the square for the expression inside the square root: \begin{align*} x^2+10x+24 %&=x^2-6 x\\[5pt] &=x^2+10x+(5^2-5^2)+24\\[5pt] &= \left(x^2+10x+25\right) - 25 + 24\\[5pt] &= (x+5)^2-1 \end{align*}

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get \[ \int_{\sqrt 2-5}^{-3} \dfrac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{x^2+10x+24}}\, \textrm{d}x = \int_{\sqrt 2-5}^{-3} \dfrac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{(x+5)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x . \]

This resembles the basic integral for inverse secant: \[ \int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}} \, \textrm{d}u = \textrm{arcsec} \, u +C \]

The only difference is that instead of $u$ as the variable, we have $x+5.$

So, let's perform the substitution \[ u=x+ 5. \]

Differentiating, we get \[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u. \]

Let's use the table below to change the limits from $x$ to $u.$

$x$ $\sqrt 2-5$ $-3$
$u$ $\sqrt {2}$ $2$

Therefore, \begin{align*} \int_{\sqrt 2-5}^{-3} \dfrac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{x^2+10x+24}}\, \textrm{d}x &= \int_{\sqrt 2-5}^{-3} \dfrac{60}{|x+5|\sqrt{(x+5)^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{\sqrt 2}^{2} \dfrac{60}{|u|\sqrt{u^2-1}}\, \textrm{d}u\\[5pt] &= 60\textrm{arcsec }{u} \, \bigg|_{\sqrt 2}^{2}\\[5pt] &=60\left(\textrm{arcsec}{\left(2\right)}-\textrm{arcsec}{\big(\sqrt 2\big)}\right) \\[5pt] &= 60\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3} -\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\\[5pt] &= 5\pi. \end{align*}
